newsitem.title: INDIA: India, China vow to turn sights to 21st century.
newsitem.headline: India, China vow to turn sights to 21st century.

text.p: India and China on Tuesday pledged to look to the 21st century in a cooperative spirit as they ended a fresh round of talks towards settling a stubborn border dispute that led to war in 1962.

Indian Foreign Secretary K. Raghunath and Chinese Vice Foreign Minister Tang Jiaxuan led the two-day meeting of a joint working group set up in 1988 to ease tensions over their 4,500-km (2,800-mile) border.

The Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement that the two sides reaffirmed that "a constructive and cooperative relationship oriented towards the 21st century...would be in the fundamental interests of the peoples of the two countries".
It said the two nations' leaders shared a commitment to "mutually beneficial relations in all areas".
The talks were part of a broader, long-standing effort by the neighbours to look beyond differences towards common ground and a more stable relationship.

India has had mixed success in trying to apply the same strategy to Pakistan, which has historically sought to focus on its dispute with New Delhi over Kashmir as the overriding, "core" issue to be resolved before addressing other disputes.
China is a declared nuclear power. India exploded an atomic device in 1974 but says it has no nuclear weapons, but Western experts say it could quickly assemble one.
Between them, China and India have one third of the world's population.
Tensions along the long border led to a brief war 35 years ago. China claims large parts of Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim, both states in northeastern India.
Sikkim is strategically vital to India as it borders Tibet. It was annexed by New Delhi in 1975 after its legislature voted to abolish the monarchy and join the Indian union.
New Delhi says Beijing occupies about 33,000 sq km (13,000 sq miles) of the Aksai Chin region that it says is part of India's Jammu and Kashmir state.
During a visit to New Delhi last November by Chinese President Jiang Zemin, the two nations agreed to reduce troops and armaments along their Himalayan boundary.
The pact fleshed out an agreement in principle signed by former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao in Beijing in 1993.

At this week's meeting, "the two sides agreed that the high-level political dialogue had played a significant part in promoting understanding between the two countries and that the momentum of high-level visits should be maintained".

The leader of the Chinese delegation conveyed an invitation from Jiang to his newly elected counterpart in India, K.R. Narayanan, to pay a state visit to China next year, the Foreign Ministry statement said.

Another invitation was extended to Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral to visit China "at a mutually convenient time", it said without specifying any dates. Tang paid a courtesy call on Gujral on Tuesday.
The two delegations reviewed military confidence-building measures along the line of control separating the two countries that had been agreed during Jiang's visit to India last year.

They also agreed to promote closer cooperation between their foreign ministries, and that the Indian foreign secretary -- the highest-ranking civil servant in the Foreign Ministry -- would visit China early next year.
